\chapter{Marks Above, Below, and Beside the Letter}
\label{ch:marks-runway}
\hlchaptermodality{5}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can write and name the six Devanagari marks the rest of this book leans on, and say where each one sits relative to its letter.}

Retrieve all six marks cold, by name and by placement, with no model on the page.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[i]{\mr{ि} — short \emph{i}, written before, read after}

\label{lesson:MR-W05-i-matra}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{dhanyavād} once from memory. Every mark in this chapter hangs on a consonant your hand already knows.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{ि}
\end{quote}

The short-\emph{i} mark is the one that breaks the rule you would guess. It is \textbf{written to the LEFT} of its consonant and \textbf{read to the RIGHT} of it: \textbf{\mr{कि}} is \emph{ki}, never \emph{ik}. The eye meets the mark first; the ear meets it second.

Draw the upright on the left of the letter, then carry the curve up and over the headline so it hooks back to the right. The hook is what tells this mark apart from its long partner, which you will meet later.

\subsection*{Writing — observe and trace}
Keep \textbf{\mr{कि}} in front of you. Trace the mark alone twice, then trace it beside \textbf{\mr{क}} twice more. Say \emph{ki} each time your pen finishes the hook, so the hand and the ear learn the same order the page will use.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which side of \textbf{\mr{क}} does the mark sit on? (\textbf{The left.}) Which side do you hear it on? (\textbf{The right.})

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0900.pdf}{Unicode Devanagari chart}, U+093F.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[u]{\mr{ु} — short \emph{u}, a small hook below}

\label{lesson:MR-W05-u-matra}



\begin{quote}
One mark went to the left. This one goes straight down, and it is the mark you will meet most often of all.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{ु}
\end{quote}

The short-\emph{u} mark is a small hook tucked \textbf{under} the letter, opening to the right. It hangs from the foot of the stem, not from the headline.

\textbf{\mr{तु}} is \emph{tu} — the opening syllable of the polite \emph{tumhī} you already say. Start at the base of \textbf{\mr{त}}, dip below the line, and curl right. Keep it small: its long partner is the same hook drawn deeper.

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy}
Copy \textbf{\mr{तु}} twice with the model visible, saying \emph{tu} as the hook closes. Then write the short-\emph{i} mark once beside it from memory and check it still leans left.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Above the line, below it, or beside it? (\textbf{Below.})

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0900.pdf}{Unicode Devanagari chart}, U+0941.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ū]{\mr{ू} — long \emph{ū}, the deeper hook below}

\label{lesson:MR-W05-uu-matra}



\begin{quote}
You have the short hook. The long one is the same gesture, carried further.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{ू}
\end{quote}

Long \emph{ū} is the short hook drawn \textbf{deeper and turned back on itself}, so it finishes pointing down-left rather than right. Same place, same start, more travel.

\textbf{\mr{दू}} is \emph{dū} — the first syllable of the word for milk. Say \emph{tu} and \emph{dū} one after the other and you can hear the length the extra travel is paying for.

\subsection*{Writing — delayed copy}
Look at \textbf{\mr{दू}} for five seconds, cover it, and write it once. Uncover and compare the depth of the hook against the short one you wrote a moment ago. Repair only if the two look the same.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\emph{tu} or \emph{dū} — which hook travels further? (\textbf{dū.})

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0900.pdf}{Unicode Devanagari chart}, U+0942.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ṛ]{\mr{ृ} — the vocalic \emph{r} mark, said \emph{ru}}

\label{lesson:MR-W05-ru-matra}



\begin{quote}
A third mark below the line. This one is not a vowel you have a letter for in English.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{ृ}
\end{quote}

This mark writes a sound Sanskrit treated as a \textbf{vowel made of r}. Marathi speakers say it \emph{ru}, so \textbf{\mr{कृ}} is heard as \emph{kṛ}, close to \emph{kru}.

The shape is a small curl below the letter that opens to the left — the mirror of the short-\emph{u} hook, and that mirroring is exactly how to remember it. It appears in tatsama words the language borrowed whole, like \emph{kṛtī}, \textquotedblleft{}activity\textquotedblright{}.

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy}
Copy \textbf{\mr{कृ}} twice with the model visible. Then put the short-\emph{u} hook beside it and check that the two curls open in opposite directions.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does a Marathi speaker say this vowel? (\textbf{ru.})

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0900.pdf}{Unicode Devanagari chart}, U+0943.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ã]{\mr{ँ} — the moon holding a dot}

\label{lesson:MR-W05-candrabindu}



\begin{quote}
You already write one nasal mark above the headline. Here is its second, softer cousin.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{ँ}
\end{quote}

The \textbf{candrabindu} is one dot cradled in a small upward crescent — a moon holding a dot, which is exactly what its name says.

Set it beside the anusvāra you already write:

\textbf{\mr{ं}} closes the vowel onto a nasal consonant. \textbf{\mr{ँ}} leaves the vowel open and sends the air through the nose while you are still saying it. Draw the crescent first, sitting on the headline, then place the single dot inside it.

\subsection*{Writing — observe and trace}
Trace \textbf{\mr{ँ}} twice, then trace \textbf{\mr{ं}} once beside it. Point at which of the two carries a crescent. Repair only the mark that came out wrong.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the two nasal marks has a moon under it? (\textbf{The candrabindu.})

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0900.pdf}{Unicode Devanagari chart}, U+0901.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[a]{\mr{अ} — the vowel your consonants have been hiding}

\label{lesson:MR-W05-a-independent}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\mr{क}} on its own. You did not say a bare \emph{k}. Something came after it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{अ}
\end{quote}

Every Devanagari consonant carries a short \emph{a} inside it unless a mark or a halant takes it away: \textbf{\mr{क}} is \emph{ka}, not \emph{k}. \textbf{\mr{अ}} is that same hidden vowel written out on its own, for when a word begins with it and there is no consonant to hide inside.

You already write its long partner \textbf{\mr{आ}}, and the relationship is visible: \textbf{\mr{आ}} is \textbf{\mr{अ}} with one upright added on the right. Draw the left loop, the vertical stem, then the headline that ties them together.

\subsection*{Writing — delayed copy}
Look at \textbf{\mr{अ}} for five seconds, cover it, and write it once. Then add the upright and check that you have made \textbf{\mr{आ}}. If the two came out identical, the upright is missing.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\mr{क}} say on its own? (\emph{\textbf{ka}} — the vowel is already inside.)

Source: \href{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Devanagari\_\%E0\%A4\%85\_stroke\_order.svg}{Saurmandal, Devanagari a stroke order}.
\end{tcolorbox}
